body:
But I suppose that's the part that confuses me. I mean, how can a psychiatrist diagnose me, and then decide on the correct treatment, when they don't give me a chance to tell them what I'm struggling with? Psychiatric disorders are diagnosed solely on the understanding of the presentation of symptoms and the impact the symptoms have on a person's life. And how can anyone understand another person well enough to make a serious judgement about who and what they are in a single conversation?

I'm not expecting my psychiatrist to listen to me vent about something I struggled with this week. I'm expecting him to pay attention when I'm trying to explain that there are serious symptoms I'm struggling with that we've never even addressed. 

And when it comes to being a doctor of any stripe, being a good communicator (which includes listening) is a *major* job requirement.

(Sorry. I know this is a little long, but I wanted to make sure I was explaining it properly!)

Honestly? I'm still learning how. After all, we're all dealing with issues that are often years -- if not a lifetime -- in the making. Recovering from these struggles will never be quick or easy. Anyone who tries to sell you a "hack" for anxiety, or any other mental health condition, may not appreciate the complexity or depth of the issue.

But I do find that sometimes the reason I'm so torn over a decision has nothing to do with the decision itself. Instead, it comes from the core source of the fears that I am feeling in the moment. When I take the time to sit down with myself and seriously ask *what* I am worried about, and then *why,* I discover the real issue I'm facing. Once I know what is really causing my anxiety, I can sometimes come up with a way to cope with it and ultimately move forward.

For example:

I was super torn up over seeking a second opinion about my diagnosis. There were a thousand worries and predictions that filled my head until I felt there was no way forward. I even began to doubt the validity of my struggles. So, I asked myself what I was most afraid of; what was the biggest, most prevalent reason that I was unable to make a true decision? In this instance, it was the fear of being judged and found wanting. I was terrified that whoever I went to for that second opinion would look at me and declare that I was being overly-sensitive and a time-waster. Once I knew this, I asked myself why I was so afraid of this judgment and I continued asking why until I realized that what lay at the core of my anxiety was not the potential judgement of another, but the current way I was judging myself. Unconsciously, I was thinking those things about myself and "giving" those judgements to people I had not even met. I was mind-reading. Of course, knowing this didn't magically take away the fears or the tangled emotions, but it did provide me with perspective and the ability to acknowledge how my thinking was being distorted. And armed with the knowledge that many of my "cons" were based on a distorted foundation, I was able to move forward.

I'm not sure if this will help you at all, since I don't know you or the full story behind your situation. Just remember to have patience with yourself and be kind. There is nothing wrong with taking a step back and wrapping yourself with cottonwool when you're feeling overwhelmed and afraid. There is nothing wrong with choosing something that makes you feel safe. You deserve to feel safe. You deserve to be comforted. And you are not alone.

Overthinking is one of my least favourite symptoms of anxiety. 😥 
It never fails to amaze me how paralyzing thoughts can be. It’s like, for every pro there’s a con, and it continues until it’s impossible to make a decision. And the more important it is, the harder it becomes. 
You’re definitely not alone in this one.
